Riyadh’s Warning Sirens

Saudi Arabia woke its capital with alerts for a “hostile aerial threat.” Then came two booms in western Riyadh, smoke near King Khalid International Airport, and major flight delays. 

By Saturday afternoon, the authorities had issued an all-clear. They did not explain what caused the explosions.

The alarms were the first in Riyadh in months. Saudi Civil Defense also activated early-warning systems in nine other cities, while a Reuters journalist heard the blasts in the Olaya district. 

The Saudi government’s media office did not immediately comment, and the Houthis made no public claim.

The timing supplied the context. Hours earlier, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the movement had thwarted unspecified Saudi “criminal attempts” in Sanaa and would respond. 

The Houthis say Saudi aircraft have carried out hundreds of strikes in recent days. Riyadh says Houthi attacks have hit civilian and energy infrastructure. 

The UN Security Council condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes that injured civilians, women and children among them.

Since July, the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at Saudi military bases, ports and airports, and declared a naval blockade against Riyadh. 

This month they seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, placing the Bab el-Mandeb choke point under a new kind of pressure. 

Saudi officials are trying to make Riyadh look like a capital with a future-investment summit on its calendar. The warning sirens gave the city a different itinerary.

No one has publicly identified the source of Saturday’s explosions. The smoke, delayed flights and emergency alerts had already done the political work: the Yemen war reached the Saudi capital’s airport perimeter.

🌐 Coldcard hacker uses THORChain to swap stolen BTC 

📣 A hacker associated with the third wave of Coldcard wallet thefts began converting stolen Bitcoin into Ether through THORChain on Sept. 3, according to Galaxy Research’s Alex Thorn. The transactions moved approximately 10% of the Bitcoin controlled by that attacker. Roughly 90% remained at its original addresses when he published the update. 

🔖 Researchers traced the swaps through THORChain to a newly identified Ethereum address. Thorn said he shared the address with law enforcement, crypto companies and other organizations monitoring the stolen assets. However, not every transaction succeeded. Thorn said the hacker appeared to be experiencing technical problems while attempting to process the swaps.

🔔 The cause of the refunds was not immediately confirmed. Possible explanations include liquidity limitations, transaction settings or protocol safeguards, but no verified technical assessment had established the reason. The movement represented the first detected onchain transfer from the original addresses associated with the first three attack waves, according to Thorn. Analysts will now monitor whether the resulting ETH moves to centralized exchanges, bridges or privacy services.
